h1: Franchising a brewpub concept and when it actually works
title: Franchising a brewpub concept | Craft Beer School
desc: When franchising a brewpub concept works in India and when it does not: consistent beer, licences per site, brewer training, royalties and brand control.
teaser: A successful brewpub tempts its owners to multiply it. Franchising looks like the cheap way to do that. It is rarely that simple.
standfirst: Restaurant brands franchise all the time. Brewpubs are harder, because every site has to brew its own beer to the same standard under its own licences. Here is what franchising a brewpub involves and the conditions under which it can work.
sections:
In franchising, the brand owner (franchisor) lets an investor (franchisee) open a venue under the brand, using its recipes, systems and design. The franchisee puts up the capital and runs the site. The franchisor earns an upfront fee and an ongoing royalty and provides training and support.

For a café chain, the product arrives in boxes from a central kitchen. For a brewpub, the main product is made on site, by a brewer the franchisee hires, on equipment the franchisee buys. That one difference shapes everything that follows.

In most Indian states, a brewpub or microbrewery licence lets you brew and sell beer on that premises. Moving beer between outlets is restricted or not allowed. So each franchise site brews its own beer. The flagship lager in one city and the same lager in another are separate batches, on different kit, with different water and a different brewer.

Keeping those beers consistent is the core of the business. If customers find the wheat beer tastes different in each outlet, the brand stops meaning anything. Read our guide on flagship beer strategy to see why the core range carries so much weight.
What the franchisor has to supply

• Recipes written as specifications, with target original and final gravity, bitterness, colour, pH and dissolved CO2, not just a list of ingredients.
  • Water profiles and treatment, because a borewell in one city and a municipal supply in another produce different beer from the same recipe.
  • Approved raw materials and suppliers, or central purchasing of malt, hops and yeast.
  • Brewer training and audits, including tasting panels that compare beer across outlets.
  • Equipment specifications so every brewhouse can actually hit the recipe.

Without these, a franchise brewpub is just a licence to use a name.

Every franchise site needs its own excise licences, fire, building and food approvals, all in the name of the entity that runs it, usually the franchisee. Rules, timelines and costs vary by state, so a franchise network across several states deals with several different excise systems. The franchisor cannot speed this up much. Franchisees need to budget for long setup times.

Franchising tends to work better when several conditions hold together. The original brewpub has run profitably for some years, not months. The recipes and processes are documented well enough that a trained brewer elsewhere can reproduce them. The franchisor has a quality team, not just a founder who tastes everything. And franchisees bring capital and hospitality experience, not just enthusiasm.

It also helps if the concept is about more than beer: a clear food menu, a design identity and service standards that customers recognise. Our comparison of brewpub and microbrewery models helps clarify what you are actually replicating.

It struggles when the first outlet's success depends on its location or one brilliant brewer, when the books are not clean enough for a franchisee to trust the projections or when the royalty leaves the franchisee too little margin. Our guide to taproom economics shows how thin margins can be once rent and staff are paid. A royalty comes off the top.

Alternatives exist: company-owned second outlets, management contracts where you run a venue an investor owns or a licensing deal for a single partner. Each keeps more control than full franchising.
Running the quality system across sites

Once there are two or three outlets, the franchisor needs a routine. Each site sends samples of the core beers on a set schedule. A central panel tastes them blind against a reference sample. Lab numbers such as gravity, bitterness, colour and pH are logged in one shared sheet. A site that drifts gets a visit, not just an email.

This costs money every month. Budget for it inside the royalty, because the day the franchisor stops checking is the day the beer starts drifting.

A franchise agreement sets fees, royalties, territory, quality standards, audit rights, training, supply terms and what happens if standards slip or either side wants out. It needs a lawyer who knows franchising and the liquor trade. Do not use a restaurant template unchanged.

Before any of that, the business model of a single outlet has to be understood in detail. That is the foundation a franchise is built on.
faqs: Can a brewpub be franchised in India?
Yes, but each site usually brews its own beer under its own licences, so consistency and quality systems matter more than in restaurant franchising.
Can a franchisor supply beer to franchise outlets?
In most states brewpub licences restrict moving beer between premises, so each outlet brews on site. Check the rules in each state.
What does a franchisee need to bring?
Capital, hospitality experience and the ability to secure licences and approvals locally, plus a brewer the franchisor can train.
Company-owned outlets, management contracts or a single licensing partnership, each of which keeps more control over the beer.
